# Authoring Lessons Log

> **Status**: Accepted | **Updated**: 2026-07-25
> **Serves**: [A11](./capability-register.md) (structural quality tools across the corpus)
> **Validated by**: `uv run python scripts/check_lessons_log.py`

<!-- -->

> **Note on this first landing.** The lessons below were learned building a
> three-book 16+ gamebook series (the Wyrmreach chain), and several `Ref` cells
> cite that series' spec, skeleton, and filled-story artifacts. Those artifacts
> are **not** part of this change: they land in a separate follow-up push so the
> process and tooling work can be reviewed on its own, alongside the other
> in-flight revisions to story development. Every lesson and every tooling change
> here stands without them; the story-dependent tests skip until they arrive
> (6 skips in the suite today), and the two Wyrmreach design and report documents
> are included because they are the evidence base each lesson cites.

Every story development run appends here. The point is that a lesson learned once becomes a
**change to the tooling** rather than folklore an author has to rediscover, so each row carries a
proposed change and a status that tracks whether it landed.

## How to use this log

**When to append.** At the end of any authoring run: a new story or series book, a skeleton
promotion, a fill pass, or a validator/gate change made in service of authoring. If the run
produced no lesson, append nothing; an empty run is a real outcome.

**What counts as a lesson.** Something a future author or a future tooling change should act on.
Three tests, any one of which qualifies it:

1. It cost real iteration to discover (a rule interaction, a calibration, an ordering constraint).
2. The tooling let a defect through, or reported it in a way that did not point at the cause.
3. It would be re-learned from scratch by the next person, because nothing in the repo records it.

A one-off typo is not a lesson. "The gate reports band membership, so the floor reads as a pass"
is.

**Fields.**

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `ID` | `AL-NNN`, sequential, never reused or renumbered. |
| `Date` | ISO date the lesson was recorded. |
| `Source` | The run that produced it (story slug, series book, or workstream). |
| `Category` | One of `validator`, `tooling`, `authoring-craft`, `scale`, `metadata`, `process`, `docs`, `product`. |
| `Lesson` | What is true, stated so it is actionable without reading the source run. |
| `Proposed change` | The change that would stop this recurring, or `none (craft note)` when the lesson is guidance rather than a code change. |
| `Status` | `open`, `accepted`, `applied`, `rejected`, or `superseded`. |
| `Ref` | Commit, PR, file, or doc. **Required** when status is `applied`, `rejected`, or `superseded`. |

**Review cadence.** Sweep the `open` rows whenever a phase is planned. An `open` row that has
survived two phase boundaries is either genuinely low value (mark it `rejected`, with the reason in
`Ref`) or it is real debt being avoided; either way, decide rather than let it sit.

**Status discipline.** `accepted` means the change is agreed but unbuilt, and it must appear in a
plan somewhere. `applied` means the change is merged and the `Ref` proves it. Nothing moves to
`applied` on the strength of intent.

**Catalog counts inside a row are dated by that row's `Date`.** A lesson that says "20 of 61 skeletons"
records what a sweep returned on the day it ran, and is never rewritten when the catalog grows; current
totals live in [catalog-census.md](./catalog-census.md) (`UW-G24`).

**A count a row *quotes* from somewhere else keeps its own date, not the row's.** A lesson that
re-measures a prior claim carries two figures, and only the new one belongs to the row's `Date`.
Give the quoted figure its source date inline, or mark it `undated` when the source never carried
one. Without that, the rule above silently backdates the quoted figure to the day the row was
written, which is the error the row exists to correct.

When a `#VERIFY` citation is checked only after a repair, on request, whether from a live run or a working copy, that check answers the CURRENT state and cannot refute a claim about a PRIOR, already-repaired state; verifying a historical claim requires the pre-repair evidence (hook output, or a commit before the repair), not a fresh run. | open | `UW-C386` |
| AL-634 | 2026-08-26 | Moderation backlog investigation (12 in-review books, 2,916 fail-safe nodes) | tooling | **Two guards that read the same input and share the same predicate are one guard wearing two coats: the failure that disables one disables the other at the same instant.** `core/config.py::_require_real_reviewer_outside_local` and `moderation/pipeline.py`'s gap-G1 mock stamp were both gated on `environment != "local"`, and both read `review_provider` and `environment` from the process environment through the same `Settings` object, which declares no `env_file` and reads nothing but exported variables. A process started without them exported takes `review_provider="mock"` (the config default) and `environment="local"` from one absence, so the config guard does not raise AND the stamp does not apply, and the pipeline writes `reviewer_independent: true` over nodes no reviewer judged. Reproduced on a workstation whose `.env` named a real provider and a remote database: resolved settings were `environment=local`, `db host=localhost`, `review_provider=mock`, `openai key set=False`. The `.env` file was a red herring; the app never reads it, so naming the keys there changed nothing and only exporting them does. This is the mechanism behind the 12 books; a `defense in depth` reading of the two guards was false from the day the second one shipped. | Make the stamp unconditional (a mock review is not independent in `local` either), so its liveness no longer depends on the same input the guard it backs depends on. **Correction, 2026-08-27 (PR #769 review):** this row originally justified that as safe because "the stamp is verdict-neutral so it never gates". Half of it does gate. The ADVISORY finding never gates, but `reviewer_independent = False` makes `moderation_report_unusable` return True on its own, and `publishing/service.py` then refuses the approval with no `override_reason` path, so a story moderated locally with the mock is permanently unapprovable. That is the intended posture, not a side effect, but it is a consequence and not a neutrality. More generally, when adding a second guard for a failure the first already covers, check whether it keys on the same input; if it does, it is not a second guard. | open | `UW-C387` |
| AL-635 | 2026-08-26 | Moderation backlog investigation (the five `genuinely moderated` books) | validator | **A stage's choice of fail-safe verdict decides whether its own outage is visible, and the safe-looking choice is the invisible one.** Stage 1 safety fails safe to `FLAG`, so a parse failure gates and renders as a flagged passage a human reads. The soft stages fail safe to `PASS`, so a parse failure is persisted as `verdict: "pass"` and then dropped by every consumer that filters PASS, including `api/review_surface.py`. `sk_clocktower_cipher` carries real `llm_safety` verdicts on all 25 nodes and a fail-safe `llm_readability` result on 22 of them, and renders as a clean, fully-reviewed surface. `moderation_report_unusable()` does not catch it either: it answers a whole-report question and returns `False` at the first genuine finding, so a report can be `usable` and 88% unjudged at once. Four of the five books called `genuinely moderated` in the first census are in this state. | Count the hidden remainder explicitly (`moderation/report.py::legacy_hidden_fail_safe_node_counts`, named `hidden_fail_safe_node_counts` when first written) and render it as one story-level structural finding, excluding gating fail-safes so one outage is not described twice. More generally: a fail-safe value that collides with the `everything is fine` value is not fail-safe, it is fail-silent; pick a distinguishable one, or carry the fail-safe fact in a field the consumer cannot filter away. | open | `UW-C388` |
| AL-636 | 2026-08-26 | Moderation backlog investigation (test fallout from the unconditional stamp) | tooling | **A test that declares one dependency in settings while injecting a different one through a seam passes until some guard reads the settings, and then fails for a reason that has nothing to do with what it measures.** Three tests declared `review_provider="mock"` (to satisfy config's own validation) while injecting a real responder through the review seam or a real provider object. Making the mock stamp unconditional made those declarations load-bearing, and the tests began failing on `reviewer_independent` and on a `pipeline`-category finding they never intended to assert about. Nothing was wrong with the fix or with what the tests measure; the declarations were simply fiction that nothing had yet read. The same shape recurs whenever config is treated as boilerplate to get past rather than as an input under test. | Make a test's declared settings agree with what it actually injects (`review_provider="openrouter"` where an openrouter provider is injected), or, where the declaration must stay a stand-in, exclude the resulting artifact by its stable contract (`concern == "mock_reviewer_active"`) with a comment saying why, rather than by a message string. Both patterns are now in `tests/unit/test_moderation_pipeline.py` and `tests/unit/test_remoderate_books.py`. | open | `UW-C389` |
| AL-637 | 2026-08-27 | PR #769 review (finding C2) | tooling | **A row-scanning detector goes blind the day the rows it scans stop being written, and it reports "nothing found" rather than "cannot tell".** `moderation/report.py::hidden_fail_safe_node_counts` located fail-safe stages by walking `findings` for PASS rows whose message carried the fail-safe substring. Since `0396507b` (2026-08-14) `ModerationReport.to_dict` no longer persists PASS findings as rows at all; it tallies them into `aggregate.pass_counts`. On any report written after that commit the scan therefore reads zero candidate rows and returns an empty dict, which the caller renders as "no stage fell back". The scan was built against the 12-book backlog, every one of which predates the change, so its tests and every manual check confirmed it working on exactly the corpus where it still works. An empty result meant three different things at once: nothing fell back, the rows were too corrupt to classify, or the report shape moved out from under the scan. | Rename to `legacy_hidden_fail_safe_node_counts` so the name states its corpus, and log an explicit blind-on-modern-report line when the scan finds nothing on a report that drops PASS rows; both shipped in PR #769. The forward detector is separate work: record `aggregate.fail_safe_counts` at persist time and read that, rather than reconstructing the fact from rows a serializer is free to stop writing. Generally: when a serializer stops emitting a class of row, grep for readers of that row in the same change, because a reader that finds nothing is indistinguishable from a reader that has nothing to find. | open | `UW-C390` |
| AL-638 | 2026-08-27 | PR #769 review (findings C3 and I1) | tooling | **`urllib.parse.urlsplit` validates nothing, and `.port` is a lazy casting property, so a refusal written after the split runs never sees the input that should trip it.** `scripts/remoderate_books.py::_database_target` split the DSN and intended to return `"unparseable"` for a malformed URL. `urlsplit` accepts any string; the `ValueError` arrives only when `.port` is READ, and that read sat outside the `try`, so a malformed port raised out of the function instead of reaching the refusal, and the caller's error path printed the raw `database_url` with its password. The refusal branch was therefore unreachable for the exact inputs it existed for. A second trap rides in the same call: `.hostname` strips IPv6 brackets, so `[::1]:5432` re-renders as the ambiguous `::1:5432` unless the brackets are restored. Sixteen malformed shapes were exercised after the fix: four resolve, twelve refuse, zero raise, zero leak. | Render a DSN by whitelist, emit only the fields a real authority positively yielded, and refuse the moment any part of the split looks misplaced, with the whole split inside one `try`. Open work this lesson carries: `core/config.py:97` has the same unguarded `urlsplit(url).port` inside an always-run `model_validator`, and pydantic's `ValidationError` text quotes the offending value, so a password containing a `/` is reproducibly echoed into the error. Fix it the same way. | open | `UW-C391` |
| AL-639 | 2026-08-27 | PR #769 review (finding I8) | docs | **A citation that resolves to nothing is worse than no citation: it lends the claim authority it never had, and it costs the next reader a full-tree grep to find that out.** `scripts/remoderate_books.py`'s module docstring justified the deliberate absence of an environment guard "per plan decision 8", with the supporting words in quotation marks. Section 7 of `docs/planning/safety/moderation-review-redesign-2026-07-28.md` contains exactly seven numbered decisions, and the quoted text appears nowhere under `docs/`. Where the reasoning is the script's own, state it as the script's own rather than borrowing a document's authority for it. Tooling proposal: extend the `scripts/check_rad_citations.py` pattern to doc citations, resolving `decision N` and section references found in `src/` and `scripts/` docstrings against the file they name, so this fails at commit time instead of at review time. | open | `UW-C392` |
| AL-640 | 2026-08-27 | Reader-reported defect in published `sk_cave_of_echoes` v1 ("who is Biscuit?"), traced through the skeleton, the binding, and the fill | authoring-craft | **A theme binding that carries a descriptor is an instruction to the fill, not a guarantee the descriptor reaches prose; compression to the shortest referring expression is the default, and nothing checked it.** `skeletons/8-11/the-cave-of-echoes.json` binds `{COMPANION}` to "her dog Biscuit" and names `{COMPANION}` in the opening beat's FILL directive, so the skeleton is correct and needs no change. The defect was found by an eight-year-old asking her father a question, which was the only detector in the system. | Delivered: PN-1 (`src/cyo_adventure/validator/naming.py`, commit `83ff95da`) makes this class visible at fill time as a WARNING over the whole corpus. | AL-641 | 2026-08-27 | PN-1 implementation, latent defect surfaced while clearing a RUF001 lint finding | validator | **`str.rstrip("'s")` strips a character SET, not a suffix, and in a discovery-then-lookup rule that defect SUBTRACTS findings silently rather than misreporting them.** The possessive-stripping helper computed `_base("Jess") == "Je"` and `_base("Thomas") == "Thoma"`. Because the mention-matching regex is then built from the truncated form, it matched nothing, the mention set came back empty, and the rule's own `if not mentions: continue` skipped the name entirely: every proper noun ending in "s" was invisible to the checker, and the checker reported clean. Nothing in the calibration figures hinted at it, because a rule that under-reports looks exactly like a corpus that is fine. Fixing it to strip longest-suffix-first surfaced 18 real findings that had been hidden. | Applied in `83ff95da`: suffix-aware stripping plus `test_a_name_ending_in_s_survives_possessive_stripping`, whose docstring records that the failure hid the name rather than misreporting it. Generalisable: any rule that derives a lookup key by string surgery needs a regression test naming a member of the awkward class, because its failure mode is a smaller finding count, which no aggregate can distinguish from success. | applied | `83ff95da` |
| AL-642 | 2026-08-27 | PN-1 exemption design, measured before adoption against the known-positive book | validator | **An exemption heuristic must be measured against the defect case before adoption, because an exemption's failure mode is a finding that never appears.** The protagonist plainly needs no gloss, and the tempting cheap test was frequency: exempt a name that appears in the start node and in a high share of nodes. Measured against the one book the rule exists for, `Biscuit` is in the start node and in **64 of 64** nodes, so it scores exactly like a protagonist on both axes and any such threshold would have exempted the precise defect being hunted. The exemption instead keys on the `{~HERO:...~}` sentinel, a declaration the contract makes rather than a statistic the prose happens to exhibit. | Applied in `83ff95da`: the hero exemption reads the sentinel manifest, and the module docstring records the rejected frequency rule with the measurement that killed it, so it is not re-proposed as an obvious simplification. Generalisable: calibrate an exemption on the known positive, never on the aggregate; an over-broad exemption is indistinguishable from a clean corpus. | applied | `83ff95da` |
| AL-643 | 2026-08-27 | PN-1 corpus calibration over the 31 committed filled books | validator | **A whole-book fill defect distributes itself across a new rule's measured noise floor, where it is read as the rule's imprecision rather than as one book's fault.** PN-1 measures 130 findings over 4,542 nodes (2.86 per 100 nodes, median 2 per book, max 33, 3 books clean). Twelve of the 130 come from `out/the-sunken-temple.filled.json`, which contains **zero apostrophe characters of any kind** ("Heddas seal") while sibling artifacts carry hundreds, so its possessives read as plurals and every possessive-only mention of a name looks like a first bare mention. That is one missing punctuation mark in one fill, not twelve naming defects, and the max-per-book figure of 33 is likewise dominated by artifact quality rather than authoring. The findings were deliberately left un-unified: inferring an absent apostrophe would merge genuine plurals into possessives and hide real cases. | Add an artifact-level fill sanity check (a filled book with zero apostrophes across dozens of nodes is a fill defect, reportable as ONE finding) so a systematic transcription fault is attributed to the artifact instead of being spread across whatever rule happens to read that text next. Carried by `UW-C394`, which also covers re-deriving PN-1's noise floor once the affected artifact is refilled. | open | `UW-C394` |
| AL-644 | 2026-08-27 | Attempting to remediate the reader-reported defect in a published book | product | **A defect a real reader finds in a published book has no in-place remedy: every editing path refuses a published storybook, and the only exit from `published` is absorbing.** `api/node_edit.py` allows an edit only while a storybook is `in_review` or `needs_revision`, explicitly never `draft`, `published`, or `archived`. `publishing/state_machine.py`'s `LEGAL_TRANSITIONS` offers exactly one transition out of `PUBLISHED`, `ARCHIVE` to `ARCHIVED`, and `ARCHIVED` has no outbound transition at all, so the only way to reach an editable state is a one-way move that removes the book from the reader's library. | AL-645 | 2026-08-27 | Repairing published `sk_cave_of_echoes` v1; dry run of `retrofit_personalization.py --book-id` against production | validator | **The personalization retrofit is structurally blind to hero-name occurrences the fill invented beyond the skeleton's slot references, so a book can sit permanently half-personalized and the sweep reports success.** The retrofit reconstructs the bound skeleton and reinserts against it, so its expectation set is the skeleton's `{HERO}` references: for this book, 42 node-slots, of which it found 41 (the 42nd names `n_open`, a node id present in the repo skeleton but absent from the deployed 64-node blob, which starts at `n_start`; the fill predates a skeleton revision). The deployed blob nevertheless carried **41 literal occurrences of "Maya" across 23 further nodes**, prose where the fill named the hero on its own initiative with no slot behind it. Those 23 nodes are invisible to the sweep by construction, and re-running it would never have fixed them: it reports `41/42 tokens reinserted, eligible=True` and looks clean. The consequence for a reader is concrete: a family that personalizes the hero's name would have met their own child's name in 41 nodes and "Maya" in 23 of the same book. | Repaired for this book by wrapping every remaining bare occurrence of the pinned `default_binding` value outside existing sentinels, round-trip verified with `strip_model_sentinels` and re-derived through `build_manifest`/`verify_manifest` (manifest went from 41 nodes / 78 occurrences to 64 / 119). Proposed for the sweep itself, carried by `UW-C396`: after the skeleton-anchored pass, either wrap the residual bare occurrences the same way or report their count as a coverage finding, so a partially-personalized book stops reading as a completed one. | open | `UW-C396` |
| AL-646 | 2026-08-27 | Attempting the archive-and-reimport repair path on a book that predates a gate tightening | tooling | **A published book can be blocked by today's validation gate, which makes `import_filled_story` unusable as a repair path for any book older than the rule that now blocks it.** Running `run_fill_gate` over the deployed blob returns `blocked=True` on a single ERROR: `PL-25 opening: first decision is 1 node(s) in, under the band '8-11' floor 2`. The measurement that matters is the comparison, not the verdict: the corrected blob's finding multiset differs from the original's by exactly one entry, `PN-1: -1`, so the correction demonstrably introduced nothing. | Repaired in place instead (see `AL-647`). Proposed, carried by `UW-C397`: give the import path a repair mode that admits a blob whose finding multiset is no worse than the stored version's, which is the comparison `retrofit_personalization.py`'s invariant 5 already performs, rather than an absolute `blocked` test that permanently locks out every pre-tightening book. Until that exists, document in-place repair as the only available route for a book that predates a gate change, so the next person does not rediscover this by building a reimport that cannot land. | open | `UW-C397` |
| AL-647 | 2026-08-27 | Executing the in-place repair of published `sk_cave_of_echoes` v1 | validator | **An in-place rewrite of a nominally immutable row is only safe when some served signal changes with it; without one, every client that already cached the row is permanently stale and nothing reports it.** `StorybookVersion` is documented as immutable, and `frontend/src/offline/db.ts` was built on that promise: it keys cached blobs by `id@version` and never re-fetches on a hit. `scripts/retrofit_personalization.py` rewrote 15 published rows under an unchanged `version`, which was invisible to every device holding a download. `api/library.py::storybook_content_hash` is the answer that was built for it: a digest over the exact bytes `get_storybook_version` emits, mirroring Starlette's serialization settings verbatim so the two cannot drift, letting the client distinguish "same version, different content" from "same version, same content". An optimistic-concurrency precondition compared the stored blob against the extracted snapshot and would have aborted on any drift. Generalisable: before rewriting a row some client caches, find the invalidation signal; if there is not one, building it is part of the repair, not a follow-up. | applied | `api/library.py::storybook_content_hash` |

What makes the permission safe is invariant 3, not this guard: `_assert_only_wrappers_added` has already proven every surface byte-identical once sentinels are stripped, so a retired finding cannot be prose loss in disguise.
